_doc: In-engine cutscenes, each at least 30 seconds long when left to play (CutscenePlayer.estimate_seconds; tests/narrative_tests.gd checks every one, tests/narrative_probe.gd times one in the running game) (StoryManager queue, CutscenePlayer). Each plays at most once per save, only in the clinic, before any queued conversation, and is skippable (ESC or SKIP; click or SPACE moves on). Acts queue cs_act_<n> when they begin; beats, story-case decisions and conversation effects can queue others ({"cutscene": id}). A shot: backdrop (scene:<illustration id> | keyart | clinic | street:<location id> | black), optional card (a chapter title), optional portrait (cast id) with expr, text (typed out), optional hold (seconds after the text, default from its length). Backdrops are the full-screen cutscene illustrations (assets/sprites/cutscenes, tools/art/cutscenes_hd.py: towers, stairs, cars, table, lattice, wall_notes, money), the title key art, the clinic room, the street scenes (with today's weather) and the cast portraits.

shots.text: Caldera. The water came up, and the city went down to meet it.
The towers kept their lights on. Everything below the fortieth floor learned to live by them.
Down here nobody has a licence. Everybody has chrome that needs fixing.
Hands that grip, eyes that zoom, spines that carry a double shift. All of it wears out. All of it is still on finance.
Kaspar's old storeroom, under the Sump. A table, a lamp, a drain in the floor. Rent due Friday.
Someone is already on the stairs.
Word travels down the Valve faster than the water does. Tonight the word is your address.
Three cars in Rustline colours stop outside. Nobody gets out until she does.
Her people check the stairs, the drain, the window that doesn't open. One of them nods. Only then does she come in.
She looks at the table, the lamp, the tray of tools. She looks at you last, and longest.
The room gets quieter than a room with five people in it should be.
Mother doesn't knock.
A name is a target.
Three people said your name this week. Two were patients. One was an inspector.
A kid sells copies of your handwriting: the scrawl on a discharge slip, laminated, two credits.
On the trains they argue about you. Butcher, saint, or just cheaper than the Plaza.
The waiting bench is full before you finish your coffee. Somebody has brought their own chair.
Being known means people come. It also means people can find you.
Power always asks for something back.
Up in Meridian Heights, someone has started counting your patients.
The checkpoints scan a little slower when your patients pass. Not slow enough to complain about. Slow enough to notice.
A car too clean for the Sump parks outside. The driver stays in. The passenger doesn't.
He wipes the chair before he sits. He does it politely, like a man who has done it in worse rooms.
"Doctor. Thank you for making the time. Mine is billed."
Truth is expensive. So is silence.
Forty static cases. A trial buried in the Sump. A lattice with a part number.
The annex lights stay on all night. The intake door has no handle on the outside.
Your notes cover the whole wall now: names, dates, the same scar behind the same left ear.
She comes alone, in the rain, without an umbrella, like someone who forgot she was allowed one.
Ilse holds her cup with both hands. It doesn't help. "Sit down. I owe you something."
Everything you did comes back.
The towers went dark at nine. Down here, every window lit at once.
People you stitched up are on the stairs with torches and toolboxes. Some came to help. Some came to collect.
The crews have closed the Valve both ways. Nobody is sure yet whose side the crews are on.
You lay out every clean tool you own. It doesn't look like enough. It never has.
The whole street knows your door now. Tonight they're all coming through it.
The lattice lies in a steel tray like a nest of grey hair. It's still warm.
Bed 14 sleeps for nine hours straight. When they wake, the first thing they ask for is their own name.
You tell them. They say it twice, slowly, as if testing whether it still fits.
By noon they're gone, in a borrowed coat, with a bag of antibiotics and no forwarding address.
Somewhere behind them a tracking signal pings an empty tray, and nobody comes to answer it.
Somewhere above the Sump, someone is singing. Badly. On purpose.
You count the money twice. It comes to the same number both times. That doesn't help.
The car has no plates. The driver holds the door like a waiter.
Bed 14 doesn't fight. They look back at your door once, the way you look at a stop you'll never ride to again.
Bed 14 waves from the back seat as it pulls away. Nobody waves from those cars.
At the annex a new name goes on a clipboard. It isn't theirs.
The room is clean. The money is in the drawer. You leave the lamp on longer than you need to.
